To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

vaccination of female rats with cDNA-FhPgK/pCMV DNA vaccine resulted in a significant reduction in worm burdens and a marked increase in specific antibody responses and cellular immune responses, whereas in sheep, vaccination had no effect on worm burdens or on the immune response.
vaccination of female rats with a DNA vaccine containing cDNA encoding FhPGK induced an immune response that resulted in a significant protection against F. hepatica challenge.

the DNA vaccination of rats and sheep with the cDNA-FhPKG/pCMV vaccine was associated with sex-specific immune responses and the protective effect of the vaccine against F. hepatica was observed only in females.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a DNA vaccine for the control of F. hepatica in sheep, and we have demonstrated that the DNA construct is immunogenic in sheep.
the development of a DNA vaccine against liver fluke.
the immune responses of rats and small ruminants following vaccination with c-DNA F. hepatica vaccine and F. hepaticainfection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
vaccination with the cDNA-FhPgk/pCMV vaccine in female rats was more effective than in male rats and male sheep.
sex differences in the course of F. hepatica infections are not only due to the different immune response of the host but also due to different parasite burdens in both sexes.
vaccination of rats with cDNA-FhPGR/pCMV induces protection against F. hepatica, but the protection is sex-dependent, and the protection is not observed in sheep.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DNA vaccines are not effective in sheep, and in rats they are more effective in females.
DNA vaccines are more effective in female rats than male rats and in female rats than sheep.
DNA vaccines encoding F. hepatica antigens can protect female rats against F. hepatica, but are not protective in male rats and sheep.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immune response of rats and sheep is different and that this difference is reflected in the efficacy of vaccination.
sex differences should be considered when designing DNA vaccine studies.
sex-related differences in immune responses to F. hepatica vaccination are not a general phenomenon.
